analysis.one_liner: Requires credit bureaus to send consumers any negative information in their file, free, within 30 days.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote: after a hearing in June 1991, it sat in a House Banking subcommittee until the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Credit reporting agencies collect information about whether people pay their bills, and that information decides who gets loans, jobs, and apartments. Under the law as it stood, a consumer generally had to ask and often pay to see what was in their own file. This bill would have required the agencies to automatically mail consumers any negative information received about them within 30 days, verified and in writing, at no charge. It died in committee without a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers with errors or damaging entries in their credit files. Today the three big agencies hold files on nearly every American adult, and negative entries — many inaccurate or out of date — can block a mortgage, a car loan, a job, or an apartment without the person ever knowing. Automatic, free, written notice would let people see and dispute the damage before it costs them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers with damaged or inaccurate credit files

how_it_helps.text: Requires every consumer credit reporting agency to fully and accurately disclose to a consumer any adverse information it receives about that consumer, and its source, within 30 days [S3].
Requires the disclosure be made in writing and mailed after the agency verifies the consumer's address, so the notice actually reaches the person [S3].
Prohibits charging the consumer any fee for these adverse-information disclosures, which the bill adds as a new subsection to the FCRA's fee provisions [S3].
Directs the Federal Reserve Board to write regulations defining what counts as 'adverse information,' so the requirement covers real harm rather than trivia [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Consumer credit reporting agencies, which would bear the cost of tracking, verifying, and mailing adverse-information notices to consumers at no charge. Lenders and other businesses that supply negative data would operate under more consumer scrutiny of what gets reported.

drawbacks.text: Mailing notices about every piece of adverse information received is a compliance burden: the agencies would have to build systems to verify addresses and send written notice for each negative entry, and smaller agencies would feel the cost most [S3].
The bill leaves 'adverse information' to be defined by Federal Reserve regulation, so consumers' actual protection would depend on how broad or narrow those rules turned out to be [S2].
Some of what gets mailed would duplicate information consumers already know — a notice about a late payment the consumer made themselves — adding volume without much benefit in those cases [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: people whose files contain wrong or surprising negative entries would learn about them promptly and free, instead of discovering them when a loan is denied. The costs fall on a small, concentrated industry and largely consist of administrative notice systems. The main design weakness is leaving the scope of 'adverse information' to regulators rather than writing it into the statute. On balance, a modest, well-targeted consumer protection.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Banking Committee, sent to its consumer affairs subcommittee, got one hearing in June 1991, and then nothing happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. E. Clay Shaw Jr., a Florida Republican, introduced the bill on April 11, 1991, with nine original cosponsors from both parties [S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Banking, Finance and Urban Affairs the day it was introduced [S5].
On May 1, 1991, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Consumer Affairs and Coinage [S5].
The subcommittee held a hearing on June 6, 1991 — the last recorded action on the bill [S5].
The bill never reached a committee vote or the House floor, and died when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumer credit reporting agencies, which avoided a mandatory free written-disclosure requirement for negative information in consumer files.

sides.party_line_note: Support was evenly bipartisan — 22 Democrats and 20 Republicans among the 42 cosponsors, with a Republican lead sponsor — and there is no record of floor opposition because the bill never got that far.

industries.note: The bill would have forced the agencies to identify, verify, and mail consumers any negative information received about them, free of charge. That removes the industry's control over when and whether consumers see what is in their files, and ends the ability to charge for it. The bill's death left that control intact.

industries.industry: Lenders and businesses that furnish credit data
industries.note: Furnishers of negative data would face more consumers seeing and disputing what is reported about them, which could force more corrections. Accurate reporters would see little change.
